Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.
Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
 Mandatory 13
File
oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:25-28
oracle-init/create-user.sh:27-30

Explanation

The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component. Without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java web application with server-rendered gallery pages, multipart uploads, and database-backed image delivery. The diagrams describe the checked-in implementation and Docker Compose configuration, not a verified running deployment; all evidence paths are relative to the repository root.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Client Layer"] Browser["Browser - Bootstrap 5.3.0 and upload JavaScript"] end subgraph Application["Application Layer - Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.5.0"] Security["Spring Security - stateless HTTP Basic"] Web["Spring MVC - Thymeleaf pages and JSON upload responses"] Business["Transactional photo operations and image validation"] end subgraph Data["Data Access Layer"] Persistence["Spring Data JPA - Hibernate and Oracle JDBC"] end subgraph Storage["Database Storage"] Oracle[("Oracle Database XE 21.3.0 - photos and image BLOBs")] Volume[("Docker volume - oracle_data")] end subgraph External["External Services"] CDN["jsDelivr - Bootstrap CSS and JavaScript"] end Browser -->|"HTTP requests on port 8080"| Security Security -->|"Public reads and authenticated upload or delete"| Web Web -->|"Gallery queries, uploads, navigation and deletion"| Business Business -->|"Read and write photo entities"| Persistence Persistence -->|"Oracle JDBC on port 1521"| Oracle Oracle -->|"Persist database files"| Volume Web -->|"HTML, JSON and image bytes"| Browser Browser -->|"HTTPS asset requests"| CDN

Diagram evidence: web dependencies and platform (pom.xml:8-26, pom.xml:30-66); HTTP entry points (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-58, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-67, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-83); security (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:45-59); transactions and persistence (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-46, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:154-176); database and volume topology (docker-compose.yml:3-18, docker-compose.yml:27-45); browser CDN usage (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7, src/main/resources/templates/index.html:124-125).

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle stores both metadata and image bytes in the photos entity table; photo_data is a JPA large-object byte array, so the implemented upload and delivery paths do not use a separate image filesystem or object-storage service (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-76, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:117-166, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:57-83). Compose persists Oracle files in oracle_data and starts the application after the database health check succeeds (docker-compose.yml:14-24, docker-compose.yml:41-49). Both application profiles configure Hibernate schema creation with ddl-auto=create; a persistent database volume therefore does not imply preservation of application tables across restarts (src/main/resources/application.properties:17-21, src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:13-17). The browser retrieves Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr over HTTPS (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7, src/main/resources/templates/index.html:124). No application cache, message broker, or outbound business API client was identified in the inspected build and main source files.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Layered monolith with constructor injection: three MVC controllers share the PhotoService abstraction; its transactional implementation delegates to one JPA repository (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:24-33, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:17-27, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:22-32, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-46).
  • Database-centric media storage with Oracle coupling: images are entity BLOBs; navigation/listing queries use Oracle-specific NVL, ROWNUM, SYSDATE and DUAL rather than database-neutral queries (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:36-41, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-62).
  • Public reads with authenticated mutations: the security filter chain requires authentication for upload and deletion, permits other requests, disables CSRF and uses stateless HTTP Basic; the configured administrator is held in memory (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-59). Credential values are intentionally omitted.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicitly mapped HTTP endpoints provide gallery/detail HTML, multipart upload with a JSON result, deletion by redirect, and binary photo retrieval. Browser requests, controller/service calls, and database access are synchronous request/response operations; no messaging or inter-service HTTP API is implemented.

No additional deployment, Helm, or IaC service definitions were found in the supplied project files.

Application framework dependencies are Spring Boot Web, Thymeleaf, Data JPA, Validation, Security and JSON, with the Oracle JDBC runtime driver (pom.xml:30-79). The database container uses Oracle Express 21.3.0 XE (docker-compose.yml:3-4); it is not source-built and has no application framework dependencies.

Wire-contract details

  • Upload responses are maps, not a serialized UploadResult or full Photo. The batch envelope contains success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads; each failure item contains fileName and error. The explicit 400 response instead contains success: false and error, without the batch arrays. success is true only if at least one uploaded photo is added to the response. A successful upload triggers a separate ID lookup; an empty lookup contributes neither a success entry nor a failure entry (HomeController.java:58-106).
  • Per-file validation/storage errors normally become entries in a 200 batch response, not 400/422. Multipart parsing failures handled by the controller become 400 with "No files provided". Missing required parameter binding and uncaught exceptions may use framework error handling rather than that JSON envelope; the successful-upload follow-up lookup is not caught by the upload controller (HomeController.java:58-106; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-184). See business-workflows.md for individual validation rules.
  • Binary responses explicitly disable caching using Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, and Expires: 0, and add X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, and X-Photo-Size. They do not set Content-Disposition (PhotoFileController.java:74-83).
  • The browser creates FormData with repeated files fields, calls /upload once, and parses successful HTTP responses as JSON. Non-2xx responses produce a generic upload failure message (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:90-132). Deletion uses a POST HTML form (src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59).
  • Static CSS, JavaScript, and the bundled file under src/main/resources/static/uploads/ are resource assets, not additional controller mappings. Default framework static-resource/error handling is not counted among the five explicit endpoints.

There are no gateway-level composition DTOs or independently owned service-to-service schemas. Entity field inventories and persistence details belong in data-architecture.md; they are intentionally not duplicated here.

JSON support is declared through Spring Boot JSON/Web dependencies (pom.xml:31-35,75-79), so upload maps use Spring MVC's configured JSON message conversion (normally Jackson). No application-specific Jackson serializer, serialization override, record DTO, OpenAPI/Swagger specification, protobuf, or GraphQL schema was found in the inspected application/build sources. Photo metadata timestamps are copied into the upload map without explicit formatting in the controller (HomeController.java:76-83); a custom date wire format is not defined there. HTML responses use view names rather than JSON serialization (HomeController.java:50; DetailController.java:54).

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous HTTP and local calls: The browser invokes the same application's endpoints. Controllers call the injected PhotoService, implemented by PhotoServiceImpl, which calls PhotoRepository directly. Database communication uses JPA/JDBC, not a downstream REST API (HomeController.java:29-41,69-74; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,36-46,53-74,164-169; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-29; pom.xml:43-54). Browser async/await does not imply a server-side queue or event contract.
  • No asynchronous service transport: No broker, producer/consumer, event-bus, gRPC client, REST client, or background upload worker was found in the application sources or dependencies. Upload files are processed sequentially in the HTTP request (HomeController.java:69-91).
  • No gateway, aggregation, discovery, or client-side balancing: There is no gateway component or cross-service response composition/fallback. Detail-view photo/navigation assembly and upload metadata assembly are local service calls, not gateway aggregation (DetailController.java:39-52; HomeController.java:69-95). Compose supplies the database hostname through its service network, rather than an application discovery registry; the default non-container connection targets localhost (docker-compose.yml:32-45; src/main/resources/application.properties:9-15).
  • Resilience and timeout contract: No application retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback client, or explicit API/JDBC request timeout was found; there are no policy-specific timeout values to report. Container restart behavior is not an HTTP retry policy (docker-compose.yml:46). The client fetch has no explicit timeout, abort controller, or retry (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:102-132).
  • Error fallbacks: Gallery lookup errors render an empty gallery; detail lookup/navigation errors redirect home; deletion errors redirect with an error flash message. Photo-byte failures return 404/500 instead of placeholder images. Upload handles many per-file errors as UploadResult failures, but no controller-level catch guarantees the batch envelope for all exceptions or transaction-completion failures (HomeController.java:38-107; DetailController.java:32-78; PhotoFileController.java:37-86; PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-28,81-184).
  • Availability/startup: Compose makes application startup depend on a healthy database. Security bean creation also requires an externally supplied admin password property. Neither requirement is an API readiness guarantee; full startup/configuration details belong in configuration-inventory.md (docker-compose.yml:41-43; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-42).
  • Authentication/authorization: Spring Security uses stateless HTTP Basic. POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete require authentication; other requests are permitted. The configured in-memory account has role ADMIN, but the route rules require only authenticated(), not an explicit role check. No JWT/OAuth2 or method-level authorization is declared. CSRF protection is disabled (SecurityConfig.java:28-59). Credentials and credential values are intentionally omitted.
  • Transport security: No server TLS configuration or HTTPS-enforcement rule was found in the inspected application configuration, security chain, or Compose deployment; the application exposes port 8080. External TLS termination is not established by these sources. Browser Bootstrap dependencies are fetched over HTTPS from a CDN, which does not secure the application's own API transport (src/main/resources/application.properties:1-7; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:24-27; SecurityConfig.java:45-59; docker-compose.yml:39-40; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:7,147).

Service Communication Sequence

Primary flow: an authenticated multipart upload followed by binary retrieval. Solid arrows show synchronous requests/local calls; dashed arrows show responses, not queued events. No gateway or broker exists to insert into this flow.

Evidence: HomeController.java:56-107, PhotoServiceImpl.java:68-74,81-184, PhotoFileController.java:37-86, SecurityConfig.java:45-59. Multipart exceptions may short-circuit the upload with 400 before the depicted loop; unhandled errors can bypass its normal 200 response. These are local error paths, not circuit-breaker or retry behavior.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Operator configuration → Compose interpolation: supply required ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD before containers are created; Compose uses required-value interpolation (docker-compose.yml:7,10,36,38).
  2. oracle-db → mounted startup scripts: both scripts check required ORACLE_PWD and APP_USER_PASSWORD, default APP_USER, and connect with SQL*Plus to create the schema user if absent. create-user.sh includes an unconditional 30-second sleep; 01-create-user.sh has no explicit readiness wait (oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:11-29; oracle-init/create-user.sh:9-30). Both are mounted; repository configuration does not independently define their execution order beyond the Oracle image's startup-script handling.
  3. photoalbum-java-app → waits for → healthy oracle-db: Compose depends_on.condition=service_healthy. The Oracle health check runs SQL*Plus using the application user against localhost:1521/XE; this checks application-user database connectivity, not just an open TCP socket. Interval 30s, timeout 10s, retries 15, start period 180s (docker-compose.yml:19-24,41-43). Credentials in the command are masked here.
  4. Application startup → Spring context and datasource availability: entry point invokes Spring Boot; mandatory administrator secret is injected during context creation (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14; SecurityConfig.java:34-42). No application container health check, explicit application startup timeout, retry policy, discovery server, or config-server dependency is declared.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  1. Copy .env.example to .env, or export the named variables in the operator shell; replace example secrets with strong unique values. The template explicitly warns not to commit .env (.env.example:1-3); ignore rules cover it (.gitignore:201-204).
  2. Compose refuses missing/empty required secret inputs, then binds administrative and schema credentials to Oracle and the matching schema credential to the application. The Oracle health check also references APP_USER and APP_USER_PASSWORD (docker-compose.yml:7-20,35-38).
  3. Startup scripts authenticate as Oracle SYSTEM using ORACLE_PWD, check whether APP_USER exists, and create it only if absent. Grants are schema-oriented; the larger script lists create privileges and unlimited quota on USERS, not DBA (oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:19-43; oracle-init/create-user.sh:21-40). Existing-user passwords are not updated by these scripts, so changing an environment secret alone is not a database password-rotation workflow.
  4. Spring resolves the application database secret and administrator secret from environment configuration. The administrator account is held in an in-memory user-details manager with BCrypt encoding (SecurityConfig.java:28-42).

No managed identity/service principal, remote secret store, encrypted-property mechanism, Docker secrets binding, or automated deployment secret retrieval was found. Environment values and SQL*Plus command arguments are not repository-defined at-rest secret encryption. Test credentials are deliberately configured in test resources and are not an operational secrets source.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared photo collection, view individual images, and navigate by upload time. Authenticated users can add photos in batches and remove photos from the collection.

Evidence references below use repository-relative paths and source line numbers. This document describes observed implementation, not intended features; no secret values are reproduced.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo collection managementAn uploaded image and its descriptive information, managed as one collection item. The only persisted business entity; no explicit multi-entity aggregate is defined.Image content and metadata belong to the same photo. Older/newer photos are computed navigation neighbors, not stored relationships. No album, owner, or user relationship exists in the model.
UploadResultPhotoService / Upload processingA transient per-file outcome, not a persisted entity: either a saved photo reference or an explanation of failure.Successful outcomes refer to a Photo; the controller combines outcomes into batch feedback.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-10; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-230.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application, not a set of independently deployed business services. The following are in-process responsibilities within one bounded context.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplPhoto collection management: upload, listing, lookup, navigation, deletionPhoto; transient UploadResultPhotoRepository and the photo database; local image-header inspection
HomeControllerGallery and batch-upload orchestrationNo independent entities; composes Photo summaries and upload outcomesIn-process PhotoService
DetailControllerIndividual-photo viewing and collection maintenanceNo independent entities; uses Photo and computed neighbor referencesIn-process PhotoService
PhotoFileControllerDelivery of stored photo contentNo independent entities; reads Photo contentIn-process PhotoService

PhotoService is the common business access layer; PhotoRepository and its database are the persisted source of truth. Controllers neither own separate copies nor exchange business events. Authentication accounts are access-control infrastructure, not photo owners.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-47,154-176; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:29-33,69-95; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:23-27; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-32; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-42.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch and publish accepted photos

  1. A user selects files or drops them onto the gallery. The browser applies Client upload screening, then submits acceptable files to POST /upload. State-changing requests must pass Write authorization before reaching the controller.
  2. HomeController applies Batch presence, then processes each file sequentially through PhotoService. There is no controller-wide transaction or all-or-nothing batch requirement.
  3. PhotoService applies Server upload admission and Image inspection. A rejected file produces a failed UploadResult; ordinary per-file failures allow processing of subsequent files.
  4. For an admitted file, the service constructs a Photo, assigns available dimensions, and persists its content and metadata together.
  5. For each successful result, the controller reloads the photo by its returned identifier and collects a display summary. Failed results are collected separately.
  6. The response follows Batch outcome aggregation. The browser displays successes and failures, prepends accepted photos to the gallery, and retrieves their images separately.

An unexpected exception in the controller's successful-photo reload is not caught by the batch loop; the partial-success behavior applies to failures returned as UploadResult, not every possible exception.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-131,135-158,176-179; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-184; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:46-59.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and navigate individual photos

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController loads the collection through PhotoService and PhotoRepository using Gallery ordering.
  2. On a retrieval exception, HomeController logs the error and renders an empty collection rather than a dedicated failure page. Users therefore cannot distinguish an empty collection from this loading failure solely from the supplied photo list.
  3. Opening GET /detail/{id} loads the selected photo, then separately loads older and newer candidates under Chronological navigation. The response combines the photo with optional neighbor identifiers.
  4. The detail page displays the image and navigation controls only where a neighbor exists. A blank identifier, missing photo, or detail-loading exception redirects to the gallery.
  5. Gallery/detail images are fetched through GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController loads the same Photo and returns its stored bytes. Photo availability determines missing-content and error responses.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:52-75,215-230; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-62; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-94; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86.

Workflow 3: Remove a photo from the shared collection

  1. The detail-page delete form asks for browser confirmation; cancellation prevents that form submission, but is not a server-side approval rule.
  2. An authenticated request to POST /detail/{id}/delete enters DetailController.
  3. PhotoService first looks up the photo. If absent, it returns false; if present, it deletes the Photo, including its stored content.
  4. DetailController sets a success, not-found, or failure flash message and redirects to the gallery. There is no soft-delete state, restore operation, or ownership check in this path.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:53-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-209; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78.

No scheduled business jobs, event consumers, batch business commands, or business-data seeding routines are present in the inspected application sources. The application entry point only starts the application (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14).

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no remote business-service calls, gateway aggregations, message-based workflows, sagas, or circuit breakers in the inspected application. All business orchestration is synchronous and in-process.

  • Upload composition: HomeController calls the shared service once per file, reloads successful Photos by identifier, and separates successful display summaries from failed-file outcomes. The browser joins each summary to its content by photo identifier using a subsequent image request.
  • Detail composition: DetailController loads one Photo and two independently queried neighbor candidates, then supplies the current photo and optional neighbor identifiers to the view. All data comes from the same collection, not separate domain owners.
  • Unavailable-data behavior: A gallery retrieval failure becomes an empty list; a detail retrieval/navigation failure redirects to the gallery; an image lookup failure returns a server error, while missing photos or bytes return not found. Upload failures returned by the service become per-file feedback; deletion failures become a flash error and redirect. These are local error-handling branches, not circuit-breaker fallbacks.
  • Freshness: Image responses discourage caching and gallery-generated URLs use cache-busting timestamps, favoring fresh reads over reuse. No business cache fallback is implemented.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50,69-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-58,64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:113-120,176-179.

Business Workflow Sequence

Primary workflow: a user uploads a batch, receives per-file outcomes, and sees accepted photos. Failure branches below are local validation/persistence outcomes, not remote-service circuit breakers.

sequenceDiagram actor User as "Authenticated uploader" participant UI as "Gallery browser" participant Gate as "Write authorization" participant Home as "Upload controller" participant Svc as "Photo service" participant Photo as "Photo entity" participant Store as "Photo repository and database" User->>UI: Select or drop photos UI->>UI: Apply client upload screening UI->>Gate: Submit acceptable files alt Authentication fails Gate-->>UI: Authentication required else Authentication succeeds Gate->>Home: Accept upload request alt No files supplied Home-->>UI: Reject empty batch else Files supplied loop Each submitted file Home->>Svc: Admit and store photo Svc->>Svc: Check upload rules and inspect image alt File rejected or file reading fails Svc-->>Home: Failed file outcome else File admitted Svc->>Photo: Create collection item with content Svc->>Store: Save photo alt Save succeeds Store-->>Svc: Stored photo Svc-->>Home: Successful photo reference Home->>Svc: Reload accepted photo summary Svc->>Store: Find accepted photo Store-->>Svc: Photo Svc-->>Home: Summary else Save exception caught in service Svc-->>Home: Failed file outcome end end end Home-->>UI: Accepted summaries and failed outcomes UI->>UI: Add accepted photos to gallery end end UI-->>User: Show available success and error feedback

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-98; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-184; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-131; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:53-58.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Admission and validation

  • Write authorization: Upload and delete POST requests require authentication. Reads are public. The configured account has an administrative role, but the endpoint rule checks authentication, not a role or photo ownership. Accounts are not linked to Photos. Authentication is stateless HTTP Basic; CSRF protection is disabled. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-59.
  • Client upload screening: The browser accepts declared JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP types and files no larger than 10 MiB. Invalid files are excluded before upload; valid files from the same selection can proceed. Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-87.
  • Batch presence: A null/empty file list returns a bad-request outcome. Multipart exceptions handled by HomeController are also reported as a bad request with “No files provided,” irrespective of their underlying cause. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:63-67,100-106.
  • Server upload admission: The lowercased supplied content type must be on the configured allowlist; file size must not exceed the configured maximum and must be positive. Current application defaults are JPEG/PNG/GIF/WebP and 10 MiB per file; multipart limits are 10 MB per file and 50 MB per request. A missing content type reaches the outer generic failure handler rather than the unsupported-type result. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:40-46,85-109,178-181; src/main/resources/application.properties:24-29.
  • Image inspection: When an image reader recognizes the content, header dimensions exceeding 40,000,000 pixels are rejected. An IOException while reading bytes or dimensions rejects the file. No recognized reader leaves dimensions absent, and other inspection exceptions log a warning and allow processing to continue without requiring dimensions. The code does not enforce a successful image decode or a match between the supplied MIME type and inspected content. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:33-34,111-162.
  • Photo validation declarations: Original filename must be nonblank and at most 255 characters; MIME type must be nonblank and at most 50 characters; file size must be nonnull and positive; upload time must be nonnull. These are model validation annotations, not an explicit controller validation step. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:28-64.
  • File-count distinction: Configuration declares a maximum of ten files per upload, but neither the inspected upload controller/service nor the browser consumes that property or enforces a count limit. Do not treat ten files as an implemented business constraint. Evidence: src/main/resources/application.properties:30; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:58-91; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-100.

Decisions, lifecycle, and derived values

  • Batch outcome aggregation: A nonempty processed batch returns HTTP 200, even if all returned per-file results fail. Top-level success is true only when at least one reloaded Photo summary is collected. A service-reported success whose reload returns empty is omitted from both outcome lists. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:69-97.
  • Gallery ordering: Stored photos are listed newest first. The gallery query substitutes a generic content type for null stored MIME values; this is retrieval normalization, not upload admission. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-29.
  • Chronological navigation: Previous means an older upload, choosing the first result ordered newest-to-oldest, from at most ten candidates. Next means a newer upload, choosing the first oldest-to-newest candidate not later than database current time. Strict time comparisons exclude equal-timestamp photos; no tie-breaker is defined. Missing neighbors produce no navigation link. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:37-62; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:215-230; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:75-94.
  • Photo availability: Blank identifiers, absent Photos, or absent/empty stored bytes return not found on content delivery; other delivery exceptions return a server error. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86.
  • Lifecycle and identity: Each constructed Photo receives a generated identity and current application-local upload time. An admitted upload becomes a stored collection item; deletion physically removes it. Rejected uploads yield transient failure outcomes. There is no approval, draft, archive, deduplication, or filename uniqueness rule in the inspected model and upload/deletion paths. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-18,79-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:154-176,190-205.
  • Derived presentation: Image dimensions are extracted where possible, not mandatory. Human-readable dates and file sizes are formatted for display; there are no pricing calculations or aggregate business totals. Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:161-197; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:108-125.

Cross-cutting behavior

  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl has a class-level transaction boundary; listing, lookup, and neighbor queries override it as read-only. Each controller-to-service upload call is separate; there is no batch transaction, compensating deletion, or distributed transaction. Exceptions thrown during transaction completion can escape the service's internal catch blocks, so returned per-file failure handling is not a guarantee for commit-time failures. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,52-75,165-184,190-229; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:69-91.
  • Error handling: Uploads use UploadResult rather than typed business exceptions. Lookup/list/delete service errors are wrapped in generic runtime exceptions; their controllers apply the outcomes described above. There is no retry queue or dead-letter path in these flows. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:55-74,173-181,206-208.
  • Audit/logging: Upload rejection/success, deletion outcomes, and retrieval failures are logged. File serving also logs photo metadata and a content-byte preview. These are operational logs, not a dedicated business audit ledger or actor-attributed change history; no actual logged content or credentials are reproduced here. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:90-100,171-181,193-208; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:45-72.

Version evidence: The build declares spring-boot-starter-parent:3.5.0. Its inherited version management is published in the Spring Boot dependencies 3.5.0 POM: Boot artifacts use 3.5.0, oracle-database.version is 23.7.0.25.01, and h2.version is 2.3.232. These are metadata-derived versions, not an executed Maven dependency resolution.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The build targets Java 21 (pom.xml:23–28) and Spring Boot 3.5.0. Boot upgrades should retain alignment with its managed dependency set and Jakarta-based ecosystem. Commons IO 2.14.0 is an explicitly pinned older release outside inherited version selection and should receive an independent update/advisory review. Verify the managed Oracle JDBC driver against the actual database and Java 21 support matrix; the ojdbc8 artifact name alone does not establish incompatibility. No vulnerability scan or current support-lifecycle verification was performed.

Notable Observations

  • The parent centralizes versions for 10 of the 11 library declarations, including both test dependencies. No BOM import is declared directly in this project's dependency management; the BOM relationship is inherited (parent, dependencies).
  • The JSON starter is declared separately alongside the web starter. This warrants a potential redundancy review, but no resolved transitive graph or lockfile was available to prove overlap. BOM-managed libraries are not automatically application dependencies and are not added to the counts.
  • DevTools is an optional compile dependency, not a test dependency. The Spring Boot Maven plugin is separately declared without a version; it is build tooling, not a library node (pom.xml:95–110).
  • No logging, messaging, caching, or observability libraries are directly declared. This does not establish their absence transitively; starter internals and actual application usage were not inspected.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one persistent entity, Photo, managed through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate. Oracle stores both metadata and image BLOBs in normal operation; the test profile substitutes an in-memory H2 database (pom.xml:43-54,88-93; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-76).

Entity Model

erDiagram %% Photo Album owns the sole persistent entity; no relationship mappings exist. Photo { string id PK "UUID string; length 36" string original_file_name "non-null; length 255" bytes photo_data "nullable BLOB" long file_size "non-null" string mime_type "non-null; length 50" LocalDateTime uploaded_at "non-null; indexed" integer width "nullable" integer height "nullable" }

Photo maps to photos. Java field names are camelCase equivalents of the diagram's mapped column names; types are String, byte[], Long, LocalDateTime, and nullable Integer. The nonunique idx_photos_uploaded_at index supports timestamp ordering. IDs are initialized with Java-generated UUIDs, and upload timestamps with local application time, in the constructor rather than a database sequence/default (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-81).

There are no foreign keys, associations, join tables, cascade mappings, or bidirectional links in the sole entity. photoData has @Lob but no lazy-fetch override, and all custom repository queries select it alongside metadata; listing therefore does not use a metadata-only projection (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:39-41; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-62). UploadResult is an operation-result object, not another entity (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:3-10).

Transactions are declared on PhotoServiceImpl at class level. Photo lookup/listing and older/newer lookups override this with read-only transactions; uploads and deletes inherit the class-level transaction (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,52-70,80-81,190-202,215-228).

These are Oracle-specific native queries, not derived finders or portable JPQL. H2 context startup alone does not establish that their Oracle-specific execution is compatible with the test database: the existing test only loads the context (src/test/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplicationTests.java:7-14). Data Ownership Boundaries

One application owns one domain table in a single configured datasource per active environment. Oracle is the normal store; H2 is a test substitute, not a simultaneously maintained read replica or separate service store. Schema-user provisioning supports a distinct application schema, but the repository does not demonstrate database-per-service isolation across multiple services (src/main/resources/application.properties:9-19; src/test/resources/application-test.properties:1-9; oracle-init/01-create-user.sh:27-43).

PhotoServiceImpl directly uses the same JPA repository for reads and writes. There is no separate command/read model, CQRS store, cross-service database access, remote data-owner lookup, or aggregation-specific bulk repository method in the inspected application data layer. Photo content is persisted as database bytes rather than a filesystem/object-store reference (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:36-46,54-70,117-118,154-166,190-202; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-62).
